cards.back: Waterfall — phases run in order (plan → analyze → design → implement). Trap: it's rigid; late requirement changes are expensive because you can't easily loop back.
cards.front: A project needs requirements nailed down before any building starts, and the client can sign off once. Which SDLC approach fits, and what's the trap with it?

cards.back: Agile / iterative — build in short cycles, get feedback each sprint, adapt. It trades upfront certainty for flexibility.
cards.front: Users keep changing their minds mid-project and you need working software in small increments. Which SDLC approach, and why?

cards.back: Analysis (use cases, requirements) flowing into Design (class diagrams, ERD, architecture). Diagrams model the system BEFORE code exists — that's the point.
cards.front: In the SDLC, which phase produces use case diagrams, class diagrams, and ERDs?

cards.back: Actors are external by definition — people or systems that interact with yours. Anything inside the boundary is part of the system, not an actor.
cards.front: Use case diagram: an actor is OUTSIDE the system boundary but a stick figure is drawn inside it. What's wrong?

cards.back: <<include>> = always happens (Verify PIN runs every withdrawal). <<extend>> = optional/conditional (e.g., 'Print Receipt' only if requested).
cards.front: Use case: 'Withdraw Cash' <<include>> 'Verify PIN'. What does <<include>> mean vs <<extend>>?

cards.back: Each Student enrolls in one-or-more Courses; each Course has many Students. It's a many-to-many association — in a database it needs a junction/enrollment table.
cards.front: Class diagram: Student 1..* ── * Course. Read the multiplicity out loud.

cards.back: Solid diamond = composition: the part's life is owned by the whole (delete the Car, Wheels go too). Hollow = aggregation: parts can live independently.
cards.front: Class diagram: a solid diamond on the Car–Wheel line vs a hollow diamond. Which is composition, and why does it matter?

cards.back: Make it its own entity/table linked by a foreign key. Repeating groups violate first normal form (1NF: atomic values only).
cards.front: ERD: an entity has an attribute that can hold MULTIPLE values per row (e.g., a student's phone numbers). What's the modeling fix?

cards.back: Redundancy / lack of normalization — the same fact stored twice can diverge. Store each fact once; derive or look up the rest.
cards.front: ERD trap: you store a customer's full address as one field AND also store city separately, and they disagree. Which principle was violated?

cards.back: Primary key: uniquely identifies a row in its own table, never NULL. Foreign key: a column that references another table's primary key, enforcing referential integrity.
cards.front: Primary key vs foreign key — one sentence each.

cards.back: LEFT JOIN from Students to Enrollments/Courses — LEFT keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs. INNER JOIN would silently drop students with no enrollments.
cards.front: SQL: get every student's name with their course titles, including students enrolled in NOTHING. Which join, and why not INNER?

cards.back: INNER: only rows that match on BOTH sides. LEFT: all rows from the left table, matches from the right where they exist, NULL where they don't.
cards.front: SQL: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN in one line each.

cards.back: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM Enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 10. Trap: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping — COUNT conditions can't go in WHERE.
cards.front: Write the shape of: count of enrollments per course, only courses with more than 10. Which clauses?

cards.back: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping/aggregation. HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY. Aggregate functions belong in HAVING (or SELECT), never WHERE.
cards.front: SQL: WHERE vs HAVING — when does each run?

cards.back: A many-to-many (or one-to-many) join multiplied rows — each match fans out. Check cardinalities, and use DISTINCT only if duplicates are truly meaningless, not to hide a wrong join.
cards.front: A query returns duplicate rows you didn't expect after a join. First suspicion?

cards.back: Indexes make joins/lookups fast (no full table scans). Cost: extra storage and slower INSERT/UPDATE, since the index must be maintained too.
cards.front: Database implementation: why index a foreign key column, and what's the cost?

cards.back: Availability first (data unusable), and Integrity in the sense the data was altered without authorization. Confidentiality fails only if data was also exfiltrated.
cards.front: CIA triad: a ransomware attack encrypts the only copy of a database. Which leg(s) failed?

cards.back: Confidentiality only. Nothing was altered (integrity intact) and the system still works (availability intact). Match the leg to what actually happened.
cards.front: CIA triad: an attacker reads patient records but changes nothing. Which leg failed?

cards.back: Risk = probability × impact = 0.2 × $50,000 = $10,000 per year. That number is what you compare a control's cost against.
cards.front: Risk: a threat has probability 0.2/year and impact $50,000. Expected risk exposure? Show the setup.
A control costs $8,000/year and cuts a risk's probability from 0.4 to 0.1 on a $40,000 impact. Worth it? Do the math.

cards.back: Vulnerability = the missing lock (a weakness). Threat = the thief (who/what could exploit it). Risk = likelihood × impact of the theft actually happening.
cards.front: Threat, vulnerability, and risk — sort these: 'no lock on the server room door', 'a thief', 'the chance servers get stolen'.

cards.back: Deterrence (fences, signs, lighting) → Detection (cameras, alarms) → Delay (locks, barriers) → Response (guards, police). Layers buy time for response — no single layer is the plan.
cards.front: Physical security plan: name the layered order an attacker meets, outside-in.

cards.back: It removes easy entry/observation points and forces attackers through multiple controlled layers. Placement is a physical control, not an afterthought.
cards.front: Why does a security plan put the server room in the building's interior with no windows?

cards.back: Authentication = proving who you are (showing ID). Authorization = what you're allowed to do once inside (which rooms your pass opens). Systems need both, in that order.
cards.front: Authentication vs authorization — the bouncer version.

cards.back: The actor step that triggers it — use case flows alternate actor action → system response. A system step floating alone means the flow is incomplete.
cards.front: A use case description says 'the system validates the input' with no actor action listed first. What's missing in the flow?

description: SDLC, use case / class diagrams, ERD, SQL + joins, database implementation, and information security.
name: CNIT 182 — Systems, Databases & Security
